title: Deep belief nets and the 2006 revival
text:
CHAPTER 16. DEEP LEARNING
SECTION 16.1. DEEP BELIEF NETS AND THE 2006 REVIVAL

By the early 2000s neural networks were again unfashionable (Section 13.2). Support vector machines and boosting (Sections 14.2-14.3) had cleaner theory and equal or better results, and networks with more than one or two hidden layers seemed impossible to train: gradients vanished, and training got stuck in poor solutions. In 2006 two papers from Geoffrey Hinton's group in Toronto showed a way to train deep networks: first learn the layers one at a time, without labels, as a stack of restricted Boltzmann machines, then fine-tune the whole network. The method itself was soon superseded, but it changed what researchers believed was possible, gave the field the name "deep learning," and led directly to the breakthroughs in speech (2009-2012) and vision (2012). This section explains restricted Boltzmann machines, contrastive divergence, greedy layer-wise pretraining and the reasons it worked.

1. The problem with depth

Why were deep networks (say, 5 or more hidden layers) so hard to train in the 1990s and early 2000s?

  - Vanishing gradients (Sections 13.1 and 13.4): with sigmoid units, each layer multiplies the backpropagated gradient by s'(z) <= 0.25 and by the weights; early layers learn extremely slowly.
  - Poor initialization: with small random weights, signals and gradients shrink through layers; with large weights, units saturate.
  - Small labeled datasets: a deep network has many parameters and overfits.
  - Limited compute: training took days or weeks on CPUs.

Yet depth seemed desirable. Theory and intuition suggested that deep architectures can represent some functions far more compactly than shallow ones (the parity function is a classic example: a deep circuit of XOR gates is small, while a depth-2 circuit needs exponentially many gates), and that perception is naturally hierarchical: edges, then motifs, then parts, then objects (Section 13.3).

2. CIFAR and the small community

In 2004 Hinton began leading a program at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR) called Neural Computation and Adaptive Perception (later renamed Learning in Machines and Brains). Members included Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun, along with neuroscientists, physicists and others. The program funded a small community committed to neural networks when mainstream funding and conference interest had moved elsewhere. The 2018 Turing Award to Hinton, Bengio and LeCun recognized this persistence.

3. Restricted Boltzmann machines

A restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) is a Boltzmann machine (Section 13.2) with two layers, visible units v and hidden units h, and connections only between the layers, none within a layer. (The model was introduced by Paul Smolensky in 1986 under the name "Harmonium.") For binary units, its energy is

    E(v, h) = - sum_i a_i v_i - sum_j b_j h_j - sum_(i,j) v_i W_ij h_j

and the probability of a joint configuration is

    P(v, h) = exp(-E(v, h)) / Z

where Z is the sum of exp(-E) over all configurations (the partition function; intractable to compute for large models).

The restriction makes conditional distributions simple. Given v, the hidden units are independent:

    P(h_j = 1 | v) = s(b_j + sum_i v_i W_ij)

and given h, the visible units are independent:

    P(v_i = 1 | h) = s(a_i + sum_j W_ij h_j)

with s the logistic sigmoid. So an RBM looks like a one-layer neural network in each direction, sharing the same weights W (transposed). The hidden units act as feature detectors: each learns to respond to a pattern in the visible data.

Learning. The goal is to maximize the log-probability of the training data. The gradient has a beautifully simple form:

    d log P(v) / d W_ij = <v_i h_j>_data - <v_i h_j>_model

The first term is the average of v_i h_j with v fixed to training examples and h sampled from P(h | v), easy. The second is the same average when the model generates its own data, which in principle requires running the alternating sampling (Gibbs sampling) until equilibrium, very slow.

Contrastive divergence (CD), introduced by Hinton in 2002, approximates the second term crudely but effectively:

    1. Set v0 = a training example.
    2. Sample h0 from P(h | v0).
    3. Sample (or compute the probabilities of) v1 from P(v | h0): a "reconstruction."
    4. Compute h1 probabilities from P(h | v1).
    5. Update: Delta W_ij = eta * ( v0_i h0_j - v1_i h1_j )

(with similar updates for the biases). This is CD-1, one step of Gibbs sampling. It does not follow the exact gradient of any objective, and its theory is murky, but it works well in practice: it lowers the energy of training data and raises the energy of the model's nearby "fantasies." For a mechatronics reader, think of it as comparing what the data look like with what the model "imagines" after one round trip through the hidden layer, and nudging the weights to make the two match.

4. Stacking: deep belief nets

The key 2006 paper was "A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets," by Hinton, Simon Osindero and Yee-Whye Teh, in Neural Computation (July 2006). The idea, greedy layer-wise pretraining:

    1. Train an RBM on the data (visible = pixels, hidden = layer 1 features).
    2. Fix it. Use the hidden activations P(h1 | v) for each training example as "data" for a second RBM, which learns layer 2 features.
    3. Repeat for as many layers as desired.
    4. The stack forms a deep belief network (DBN), a generative model: the top two layers form an RBM, and lower layers are directed downward connections.
    5. Fine-tune: for classification, add an output layer and train the whole network with backpropagation (or the paper's "up-down" algorithm for the generative model).

The paper showed that adding each layer, done correctly, improves a lower bound on the log-probability of the data, giving a theoretical justification. On MNIST (Section 13.3), the fine-tuned DBN achieved an error rate of about 1.25 percent, better than standard backpropagation networks and comparable to SVMs, without using knowledge of image structure such as convolution. The network could also generate digit images by running the model "downward," showing what each class "looked like" to it.

The second paper, "Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks," by Hinton and Ruslan Salakhutdinov, appeared in Science on 28 July 2006. It used RBM pretraining to initialize deep autoencoders: networks that compress the input through a narrow middle layer (a "code") and reconstruct it. Deep autoencoders were known to be very hard to train from random initialization; with pretraining, they learned codes that were much better than principal component analysis (PCA). With a 30-unit code layer on images of faces and digits and 2D codes for document collections, the learned codes captured structure (for example, grouping documents by topic) far better than PCA or latent semantic analysis. A deep autoencoder is the nonlinear generalization of PCA: a linear autoencoder with squared error learns the same subspace as PCA.

Publication in Science brought wide attention, and the term "deep learning" took hold around this time.

5. Other routes to depth

Several groups found alternatives quickly:

  - Yoshua Bengio, Pascal Lamblin, Dan Popovici and Hugo Larochelle ("Greedy Layer-Wise Training of Deep Networks," NIPS 2006, published 2007) showed that stacking ordinary autoencoders instead of RBMs also worked.
  - Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Christopher Poultney, Sumit Chopra and Yann LeCun (2006-2007) used sparse energy-based models.
  - Pascal Vincent and colleagues (2008) introduced denoising autoencoders: corrupt the input (for example, set some pixels to zero) and train the network to reconstruct the clean input, forcing it to learn robust features.
  - Salakhutdinov and Hinton developed deep Boltzmann machines (2009).

Why did pretraining help? Dumitru Erhan, Bengio and colleagues studied this in 2009-2010 ("Why Does Unsupervised Pre-training Help Deep Learning?", JMLR 2010). Their evidence suggested pretraining acts as a regularizer and as a good initialization: it places the weights in a region from which backpropagation finds solutions that generalize better, particularly when labeled data are limited. Unsupervised learning on unlabeled data, plentiful and cheap, captured structure useful for the supervised task.

6. The speech breakthrough (2009-2012)

The first big practical success came in speech recognition. Abdel-rahman Mohamed, George Dahl and Hinton (around 2009) replaced the Gaussian mixture models in an HMM speech recognizer (Section 14.1) with a pretrained deep neural network that predicted HMM states from a window of acoustic frames, reporting strong results on the TIMIT phone recognition benchmark. Collaborations followed with Microsoft Research (Li Deng, Dong Yu and others), Google and IBM, which scaled the approach to large-vocabulary recognition. The jointly written paper "Deep Neural Networks for Acoustic Modeling in Speech Recognition: The Shared Views of Four Research Groups" (Hinton, Deng, Yu, Dahl, Mohamed and others, IEEE Signal Processing Magazine, November 2012) reported large reductions in word error rate over the best GMM-HMM systems across several tasks. Within a few years, deep networks were in the speech recognizers of major products, including smartphone voice search and assistants.

Notably, it soon turned out that with enough labeled data and good initialization, pretraining was not even necessary for speech: plain backpropagation on deep networks worked once compute (GPUs, Section 15.1) and data were sufficient.

7. Why pretraining faded

By about 2012-2014 RBM pretraining had largely disappeared from practice. Reasons:

  - Better initialization: Xavier Glorot and Bengio (2010, "Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks") analyzed how activation and gradient variances change across layers and proposed scaling initial weights so that variances are preserved (often called Xavier or Glorot initialization: variance about 2 / (n_in + n_out)). Kaiming He and colleagues (2015) adapted this to ReLU units (variance 2 / n_in).
  - ReLU activations, max(0, z), which do not saturate for positive inputs and reduce vanishing gradients (Section 16.3).
  - Large labeled datasets (ImageNet, Section 16.2) and GPUs, which made direct supervised training of large networks feasible.
  - Regularization methods like dropout (Section 16.3).

But the central idea of the 2006 work, learning representations from unlabeled data first and then adapting them to a task, returned in a much more powerful form. Self-supervised pretraining of large models on unlabeled text and images (word embeddings, Chapter 17; BERT and GPT, Chapters 18-19) is the dominant paradigm of AI in the 2020s. "Pretrain, then fine-tune" is a direct conceptual descendant of the deep belief net, even though the RBM itself is now rarely used.

8. Generative models

DBNs were generative models: they learned P(data) and could produce samples. That line continued through variational autoencoders (Diederik Kingma and Max Welling, 2013), generative adversarial networks (Ian Goodfellow and colleagues, 2014), autoregressive models, and diffusion models (from 2015, popular after 2020), which power modern image generation. The energy-based view of RBMs (learning by lowering the energy of data and raising it elsewhere) also survives in energy-based model research and in the contrastive learning objectives used to train image and text encoders.

9. Summary

  - Deep networks were hard to train in the 1990s-2000s due to vanishing gradients, poor initialization, small datasets and limited compute.
  - From 2004, Hinton's CIFAR program (with Bengio and LeCun) sustained a small neural network community.
  - RBMs (Smolensky's Harmonium, 1986) have bipartite connections, so P(h | v) and P(v | h) factorize; contrastive divergence (Hinton, 2002) approximates the learning gradient <v h>_data - <v h>_model with one Gibbs step.
  - Hinton, Osindero and Teh (Neural Computation, July 2006) trained deep belief nets by greedy layer-wise RBM pretraining plus fine-tuning; Hinton and Salakhutdinov (Science, 28 July 2006) trained deep autoencoders that beat PCA.
  - Stacked and denoising autoencoders (Bengio et al., Vincent et al.) offered alternatives; pretraining acted as regularization and initialization.
  - Deep networks transformed speech recognition from 2009-2012 (IEEE Signal Processing Magazine, November 2012).
  - Better initialization, ReLU, dropout, big data and GPUs made pretraining unnecessary, but the pretrain-then-fine-tune idea returned in self-supervised learning.
